_note: English base. Every key the assistant can emit is defined here, so a missing key in another language falls back to a real sentence rather than to nothing. Placeholders in {braces} are filled by the caller and must survive translation unchanged - they carry numbers, place names and botanical names.

assistant.help.body:
I drive this map and the engine behind it. Things that work:

**Move around** - "show me Bopal", "go to 23.03, 72.58", "take me to Sabarmati riverfront"
**Read a place** - "what's here", "how's the air", "how green is this", "what's the soil like"
**Rank** - "where should the city plant first", "top 5 cells"
**Compare** - "compare Bopal and Naranpura"
**Design** - "design a 1 hectare park for a school", "plant 60 neem here"
**Cost and horizon** - "how much would that cost", "project it 25 years"
**Judge** - "review my design"

I answer from measured data and the trained panel. Where a number does not exist I will tell you so rather than make one up.
assistant.greet.hello: Hello. Ask me what is here, where the city should plant first, or tell me to design something - "design a 1 hectare park" will draw and cost one. Say **help** for the full list.
assistant.greet.hello_where: Hello. You are looking at **{place}**. Ask me what is here, where the city should plant first, or tell me to design something - "design a 1 hectare park" will draw and cost one. Say **help** for the full list.
assistant.unknown.body:
I did not understand that, and I would rather ask than answer a question you did not put.

Try: **what's here**, **how's the air**, **what should I plant here**, **where should the city plant first**, **design a 1 hectare park**, or **compare X and Y**.
assistant.need_point: Pick a place first - click the map, or tell me where ("go to Bopal"). Everything I read is scoped to the perimeter around that point.
assistant.error.body: That one broke on my side rather than yours - {err}. Try rephrasing, or ask me 'help' for what I can do.
assistant.goto.coords: Moving to {lat}, {lon} and reading the {km2} km² around it.
assistant.goto.place: Searching for **{place}**, then reading the {km2} km² around it.
assistant.goto.which: Which place? Give me a name ("Bopal", "Sabarmati riverfront") or a coordinate pair.
assistant.view.green: Green view on. The heatmap is this-moment canopy read off the satellite tiles; the hexagons on top are the engine's 42-month NDVI forecast - amber means it is green today and predicted to lose it.
assistant.view.priority: Priority view on. Warm hexagons are where the engine ranks planting most urgent. Click one for its reasoning.
assistant.report.head: **{place}** - across the {km2} km² perimeter:
assistant.report.aqi_spread: It is not uniform - {lo} to {hi} between the cleanest and dirtiest corner, which one centre reading would have missed.
assistant.report.aqi_none: Air quality did not load for this area.
assistant.report.canopy: Tree canopy reads **{pct}%** of the surface ({verdict}), measured from the visible bands of current satellite imagery.
assistant.report.bare: About **{pct}%** of the area scans as bare, plantable ground - modelled from imagery, not surveyed.
assistant.report.rain: Rainfall averages **{mm} mm/yr**{hot}. That is what decides whether a species needs irrigation past year three.
assistant.report.census: OpenStreetMap counts {items} inside the perimeter. OSM is community-mapped and thin in Indian cities, so treat mapped trees as a floor, not a count.
assistant.verdict.unknown: Not enough loaded to call it yet - click the map again to retry the readings.
assistant.verdict.plant_room: **Verdict: this is a planting case.** Air above the moderate band with thin cover is the combination the whole engine is built to find and there is bare ground to work with. Ask me what to plant.
assistant.verdict.plant_noroom: **Verdict: this is a planting case.** Air above the moderate band with thin cover is the combination the whole engine is built to find, though bare ground is limited - this may be a street-tree and courtyard job rather than a park. Ask me what to plant.
assistant.verdict.air_only: **Verdict: the air is the problem, not the cover.** Existing canopy is holding up, so the gain here comes from buffering the source - dense-crowned, high-tolerance species along the road edge rather than a new park in the middle.
assistant.verdict.thin: **Verdict: thin cover, tolerable air.** Planting here buys shade and surface cooling more than it buys air quality. That is still worth doing in a city with 40°C days - just do not sell it as a pollution fix.
assistant.verdict.ok: **Verdict: this area is in decent shape.** Cover is present and air is inside the moderate band. The engine's ranking will point you at cells that need it more - ask me for the priority list.
assistant.air.none: Air quality has not loaded for this area yet - Open-Meteo did not answer. Click the map again to retry.
assistant.air.head: **US AQI {aqi} - {word}** averaged over {n} points across {km2} km².
assistant.air.pm25: PM2.5 sits at **{pm25} µg/m³** - {times}× the WHO 24-hour guideline of 15.
assistant.air.species_note: At this level the species choice is not cosmetic. Ask me what to plant and I will filter to the high-pollution-tolerance rows only.
assistant.air.forecast: The trained panel forecasts this cell's AQI to move **{delta}** over its 12-month horizon{tail}
assistant.cover.head: Canopy covers **{pct}%** of this {km2} km². That is measured now, from the visible bands of the satellite tiles - a greenness index, not a true NIR-based NDVI, so it undercounts in shadow and over-reads on painted surfaces.
assistant.cover.none: Canopy did not compute - the imagery tiles did not load.
assistant.cover.engine: The engine's own history for this cell: MODIS NDVI **{ndvi}** latest{trend}.
assistant.cover.decline: That is a real decline, not noise at this slope - this cell is losing cover, which is exactly what the priority ranking is built to catch.
assistant.cover.switch: Switch on the Green view to see where the cover actually is.
assistant.water.rain: Rainfall here averages **{mm} mm/yr** ({band}), from the Open-Meteo archive.
assistant.water.dry_note: Under ~750 mm you are irrigating through establishment whatever you plant. Drip cuts that roughly in half, and a native grass meadow uses about a tenth of what a lawn does - those two choices move the 25-year water bill more than the species list does.
assistant.water.none: The rainfall archive has not loaded for this area yet.
assistant.water.hot: **{days} days a year over 40°C.** Saplings die in that window, not in the monsoon - the three-year establishment budget is where survival is actually bought.
assistant.soil.none: No soil profile covers this point. The engine carries ISRIC SoilGrids v2.0 for the configured city bbox only, and SoilGrids masks built-up land, so dense-core cells can come back empty even inside it. Species matching then falls back to pollution and water need alone - which is honest, just less specific.
assistant.soil.head: Soil for H3 cell `{zone}`:
assistant.soil.caveat: These are modelled 250 m estimates, not a site test. Dig a pit before you buy saplings - but they are good enough to rule species in and out, which is how I use them.
assistant.traffic.body: Opening the traffic panel. Be clear on what it is: with no TomTom key set, congestion here is **modelled** from OpenStreetMap road topology - lane count, road class, junction density - not measured. The engine's own traffic stream is an inert placeholder with MCDA weight 0, so it never moves a ranking. Bottlenecks are still worth reading as *where a dust buffer would earn its keep*, not as a live flow measurement.
assistant.priority.none: The ranking has not been computed - the engine loaded no zones. Check the server log.
assistant.priority.head: The engine ranked **{total} H3 cells** across {city} on 42 months of MODIS NDVI and Open-Meteo AQI. Top {n}:
assistant.priority.footer: The score is multi-criteria and numeric - AQI worsening 0.40, NDVI decline 0.35, low green cover 0.15, plantable space 0.10. Traffic is weighted 0. The model writes the justification; it never reorders the ranking.
assistant.compare.need_two: Give me two places: "compare Bopal and Naranpura".
assistant.compare.body: Comparing **{a}** against **{b}**. I will read both perimeters live - air at nine points each, canopy from imagery, the OSM census - and put them side by side. This takes a few seconds per side because the census is the slow query.
assistant.species.none: No species matched, which should not happen - the knowledge base has rows for every context. Check the server log.
assistant.design.head: Laying out a **{ha} ha** ({m2} m²) {kind} at {where}.
assistant.design.tail: Drawing it now. Everything is editable - click any tree to remove it, or redraw the plot. Ask me for the cost when you want the bill of quantities.
assistant.plant.head: Placing **{n} trees** - {mix}.
assistant.plant.named_why: You asked for {species} specifically, so that is what I placed. Ask "what should I plant here" if you want the engine's own pick instead.
assistant.plant.tail: If there is no plot drawn yet I will square off a hectare at the centre first.
assistant.cost.none: Nothing is placed yet, so there is nothing to cost. Ask me to design something first - "design a 1 hectare park" - or draw a plot yourself in the Studio.
assistant.cost.body: Costing the {n} items on the plot. Every line comes from something actually placed - nothing is a percentage of a guess except contingency (12%) and design fee (8%), which are the conventions. Tree figures are all-in over the three-year establishment period, which is where the money and nearly all the survival actually goes. Rates are indicative 2026 Indian rates, not a tendered quote.
assistant.project.none: There is no design to project yet. Ask me to design something, then come back and I will run it forward.
assistant.project.body:
Running the design forward **{years} years**.

Read the label on it: this is **projected, not forecast**, and the engine marks it UNVALIDATED in the output for a reason. It is logistic canopy growth against a species survival curve and a saturating cooling effect - a defensible shape, not a prediction. Nothing in the 42 months of history can check a {years}-year horizon, and the engine's honest validation ceiling is 23 months.
assistant.review.none: Nothing placed yet - draw or ask me to design something first.
assistant.review.body: Opening the review. It checks species diversity, water load against local rainfall, canopy at maturity versus plot area, shade coverage of seating and paths, permeability, and whether anything toxic sits where children go.{note}
assistant.review.note_strong: Last score was **{score}/100**. That is a strong design.
assistant.review.note_ok: Last score was **{score}/100**. Solid, with named gaps to close.
assistant.review.note_bad: Last score was **{score}/100**. There are real problems flagged - read the critical ones first.
assistant.explain.menu: Ask me about **NDVI**, **H3**, **MCDA**, the **priority** score, the **memory** loop, **traffic**, **plantable** space, or **accuracy** and I will explain what is actually behind the number.
assistant.explain.ndvi: NDVI is the Normalised Difference Vegetation Index - (NIR - red) / (NIR + red). Live leaves reflect near-infrared hard and absorb red, so healthy cover runs 0.3-0.8 and bare ground sits near 0.1. The engine uses NASA MOD13Q1 at 250 m on a 16-day composite. The browser's Green view cannot do this - satellite tiles are RGB with no NIR band - so it computes a visible-band greenness index instead and says so.
assistant.explain.h3: H3 is Uber's hexagonal grid. Resolution 7 cells are about 5 km², which is what matches the real data density here - 250 m MODIS pixels and a coarse AQI reanalysis. Resolution 9 was tried and left 99% of the bbox empty.
assistant.explain.mcda: Multi-criteria decision analysis: each cell gets a normalised score per criterion, and the criteria are weighted - AQI worsening 0.40, NDVI decline 0.35, low green cover 0.15, plantable space 0.10, traffic 0.00. It is numeric and auditable. The language model explains the result; it never produces it.
assistant.explain.priority: The priority score is the MCDA total. Warm hexagons on the map are cells where cover is falling fastest against air that is getting worse - not simply the cells with the least green today.
assistant.explain.memory: The engine backtests: predict a past month from history strictly before a cutoff, score it against what really happened, write a one-line lesson, and retrieve the most relevant lessons into later prompts. That is in-context learning - no weights are updated, nothing is fine-tuned.
assistant.explain.traffic: There is no free historical traffic source for arbitrary coordinates, so the engine's traffic stream is an inert placeholder with MCDA weight 0. It never influences a ranking. The browser models congestion from OSM road topology, which is a different thing and labelled as such.
assistant.explain.plantable: Plantable space is a proxy - 1 minus NDVI - unless a bare-ground survey CSV is wired in, which it is not by default. The GeoJSON says which of the two produced each number in `plantable_source`.
assistant.explain.accuracy: Honest version: a 1.5B local model is worse than a trend line at numeric extrapolation - MAE 33.3 on AQI against 13.5 for the offline Theil-Sen baseline. So the numbers come from the deterministic engine and the model writes the prose. That is not a limitation being hidden, it is the design.
assistant.match.headline: Matched against {conditions}.
assistant.match.headline_none: Matched on planting goal alone - no live readings were supplied.
assistant.match.caveat_nosoil: No soil profile covers this point, so pH and texture did not filter the list - SoilGrids masks built-up land and only the configured city bbox is loaded.
assistant.match.caveat_relaxed: The soil filter left too few species to choose from, so the full table was used and soil fit is advisory here.
assistant.match.caveat_always: Species traits are indicative defaults, not verified silviculture - confirm against your state Forest Department nursery list before ordering.
assistant.why.large_crown: large crown closes an open gap fastest
assistant.why.aggressive: (roots are aggressive - keep it clear of pavement)
assistant.why.needs_room: (needs more open ground than this plot has)
assistant.plan.spacing: {spacing} m centres come from the mature crown width of the species chosen, not a round number - planting tighter means felling half of them later.
assistant.plan.mix: {n} species rather than one: a single-species planting is one pest season away from a gap, and mixed stands are what actually survive in Indian municipal plantings.
assistant.plan.open: 45% of the plot is left unplanted: paths, open ground and the space that makes a park usable rather than a woodlot.
assistant.plan.drip: At {mm} mm/yr this needs drip through establishment - it roughly halves the water bill for the three years that decide survival.
assistant.plan.tolerance: AQI {aqi} is why the mix leans on high-tolerance species rather than the showiest ones.
assistant.plan.recharge: A recharge pit is in the list because most Indian municipal codes require one above a 300 m² plot.
assistant.cell.sentence: This point falls in H3 cell `{zone}`, which the engine ranks **#{rank} of {total}** for planting priority (score {score}).
assistant.cell.trend: Its MODIS NDVI trend over 42 months is **{trend}/yr**, with forecast AQI change **{delta}**.
assistant.compound.lead: Moving to **{place}** first, then answering that.
assistant.empty.head: About **{pct}%** of this {km2} km² scans as bare, plantable ground — roughly **{ha} hectares**. That is modelled from current satellite imagery, not a land survey, and it counts anything without vegetation: rooftops, car parks and construction sites are in that figure alongside genuinely open soil.
assistant.empty.none: Bare-ground cover has not computed for this area yet — the imagery tiles did not load.
assistant.empty.cells_head: The {n} cells nearest you with the most room to plant, from the engine's 42-month panel:
assistant.empty.caveat: Two honest limits. The plantable figure is a proxy — 1 minus NDVI — because no bare-ground survey is wired in by default, so it cannot tell open soil from a warehouse roof. And none of it speaks to ownership: a cell with room is not a cell you are allowed to plant on. Switch to the Green view and the red cells are the low-vegetation ones.
assistant.carbon.none: There are no trees placed yet, so there is nothing to total. Ask me to design something first.
assistant.carbon.body:
**{n} trees** at maturity absorb roughly **{lo}–{hi} kg of CO₂ a year** between them — about **{t_lo}–{t_hi} tonnes over 25 years**.

That range is wide on purpose. Per-tree uptake in the studio's own table runs from 2 kg/yr for a shrub to 35 kg/yr for a mature Banyan, and real uptake depends on survival, water and how much of the crown actually develops. Treat the low end as the planning number: it already assumes some of them die.
assistant.heat.now: It is **{temp}°C** right now, measured across the perimeter.
assistant.heat.days: This area sees about **{days} days a year over 40°C**.
assistant.heat.canopy: Canopy currently covers **{pct}%** of the surface — that is the lever you have.
assistant.heat.mechanism: Trees cool a street two ways: shade cuts the radiation reaching the pavement, and transpiration moves heat into water vapour. Measured street-level effects in Indian cities sit around 2–4°C under a closed canopy on a clear afternoon, and near zero at night — the studio's 25-year projection models this as a **saturating** curve for that reason, and labels it projected rather than forecast. Shade over paths and seating buys far more felt comfort per rupee than the same trees scattered across open ground.
assistant.budget.ask: Give me a figure and I will work it back — "what can I do with 5 lakh" or "budget of 25 lakh".
assistant.budget.body:
**{amount}** buys roughly **{trees} trees** across about **{ha} hectares** at 9 m centres.

That comes from the studio's own bill of quantities, not a rule of thumb: about **Rs {per} per tree all-in**, which covers the sapling, the pit, the guard, and — the part most budgets miss — three years of watering and replacement. I have assumed roughly 72% of the money reaches planting and 28% goes to ground works, paths and water. Open the cost panel after designing and you will get the itemised version.
assistant.maint.none: Nothing is placed yet, so there is no upkeep to estimate. Design something first.
assistant.maint.body:
Upkeep is in the cost panel as an annual figure, separate from the build cost — that separation is deliberate, because upkeep is what actually kills municipal plantings.

The drivers, in order: watering through the first three years, a mali's time, and replacing failures. A native grass meadow costs about a quarter of a lawn to keep. Drip irrigation roughly halves the water line. Nothing in the estimate assumes a maintenance contract that does not exist — if there is no budget line for a waterer, plant drought-tolerant species and say so in the proposal.
assistant.timing.body:
In most of India the answer is **the start of the monsoon** — mid-June to mid-July for the west and north. A sapling planted then gets ten to twelve weeks of free water to establish roots before it has to survive a dry season on its own.

Planting in March or April is the common mistake: it puts a new root system straight into 40°C with no reserve, and the failure rate roughly doubles. If you must plant off-season, budget for irrigation from day one rather than hoping.

Pit preparation should happen four to six weeks earlier, so the soil has settled and any amendment has integrated before the sapling goes in.
assistant.survival.general: Realistic urban survival in Indian municipal plantings runs **60–85% at three years** when there is a watering plan, and well under half when there is not. The three-year establishment period is where the money and nearly all the mortality sit — which is why the cost engine here prices it as a line item rather than assuming it away.
assistant.survival.body:
Of **{n} trees**, expect roughly **{lo} to {hi} alive at three years** — the 60–85% band that Indian municipal plantings actually achieve when watering is budgeted.

Without a watering plan, halve the low end. The single biggest lever is not species choice: it is whether someone is paid to water through the first two dry seasons, and whether failures get replaced in year two rather than left as gaps.
assistant.people.body:
I do not carry a population layer, so I will not put a headcount on this — any number I gave you would be invented.

What I do have is a built-form proxy from OpenStreetMap: **{buildings} buildings** and **{schools} schools** inside the perimeter. Schools matter more than raw population for siting, because shade on a route children walk is worth more than shade on an arterial nobody crosses. If you need real catchment numbers, Census 2011 ward boundaries or WorldPop would layer onto this grid — neither is wired in.
assistant.sources.body:
Every figure here has one of four origins, and the interface labels which:

**Measured** — Open-Meteo for air quality and weather, sampled at nine points across the perimeter; OpenStreetMap via Overpass for the feature census; Esri World Imagery for the canopy index.
**Reanalysis** — rainfall and hot-day counts, Open-Meteo's ERA5 archive over 2020–2024. Model output, not gauge data, and not a 30-year normal.
**Engine** — NASA MOD13Q1 NDVI at 250 m and Open-Meteo's air-quality archive, 146 H3 cells × 42 months, plus ISRIC SoilGrids v2.0 for pH and texture.
**Modelled or projected** — congestion from OSM road topology, and the 25-year growth curve, which is explicitly marked UNVALIDATED.

Two things that are *not* real and are labelled so: the traffic stream in the engine is an inert placeholder with weight 0, and plantable space is a 1-minus-NDVI proxy unless a bare-ground survey is supplied.
